newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Contracts, rebels hit Colombian oil boom.
newsitem.headline: Contracts, rebels hit Colombian oil boom.

text.p: As foreign multinationals wrangle over "unprofitable" production contracts and leftist rebels launch the fiercest-ever attacks on key infrastructure, industry insiders warn that the bubble could be about to burst on Colombia's fledgling oil boom.

While contract disputes and the deteriorating security situation may not be critical enough to drive large foreign oil companies out of Colombia, industry chiefs believe both factors have conspired to slash profits and eliminate incentives to carry out vital new exploration.

Mines and Energy Minister Rodrigo Villamizar said recently that Colombia had to kickstart exploration, warning that unless major new discoveries were made before the end of the decade, the country's dream of producing one million barrels of crude a day by the year 2000 would evaporate and it would become a net oil importer by 2006.
"The industry recognises we need to have more competitive terms to stimulate exploration," said John Doust, the head of British Petroleum's Colombian unit, BP Exploration.
"The main issue with the (current production) contracts is ... the lack of incentive for private companies to explore."

BP, Colombia's largest single foreign investor, is engaged in a protracted wrangle over how to split profits with its associate, the state-run oil company Ecopetrol, from the giant Piedemonte field in eastern Colombia once it comes on stream in late 1999.

Under the existing "sliding scale" contract, profits would be split 50-50 while output remained below a total of 60 million barrels. BP would receive a decreasing proportion of the profits, bottoming out at a 30-70 split in favour of Ecopetrol, once production rises above 150 million barrels.

BP argues that difficult drilling conditions and high exploration costs would leave it with unacceptably low profit margins. Complex negotiations have left BP and Ecopetrol arguing whether the 10 trillion cubic feet of natural gas reserves or the one billion barrels of condensates so far located should be considered the benchmark hydrocarbon for the purposes of dictating the rate at which the sliding scale comes into effect.

The sliding scale contract, which governs some 20 other fields besides Piedemonte, has been superceded by the so-called Factor-R contract, under which Ecopetrol and private sector associates share some initial exploration costs.

BP, however, would like to see a return to the old-style 50-50 contract in which associates shared profits evenly -- an arrangement that it says was simple to understand and guaranteed internationally competitive margins of between 20 and 25 percent.

But Margarita Mena, who headed the Mines and Energy Ministry when the sliding scale was introduced in the late 1980s, believes foreign players' profit margins were reduced by general taxation measures, and not by the contract itself.

"The solution lies ... in modifying other factors to make Colombia more attractive to investment. To stimulate oil investment we must create stable rules of the game," she said. "The tax situation has been a disincentive for foreign capital."

Mena said Occidental had gained profit margins as high as 34 percent from Cano Limon, the largest discovery in the Western hemisphere, and subsequent contracts were revised to ensure Colombia would retain a higher proportion of its natural wealth.
More dramatic than contract problems, however, is the current wave of leftist rebel attacks on key oil infrastructure.

Foreign oil companies are traditionally secretive about security spending, including payments for non-lethal aid to the army, which has at least 11,000 troops guarding oil facilities. But industry insiders estimate an oil company's security bill adds up to 15 percent to the cost of operating in Colombia.

The country's second-largest oil pipeline, which pumps an average of about 180,000 barrels per day from Cano Limon to the Caribbean coast terminal at Covenas, was dynamited numerous times by National Liberation Army rebels since the beginning of the year.

The value of lost production is estimated at more than $4 million per day. But Occidental spokesman Robert Stewart said the security situation was unlikely to force the company out of Colombia: "We're an experienced oil company and intend to fulfil our contractual obligations with Colombia."
